newsitem.title: USA: Clinton kicks off bid for support on climate plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton kicks off bid for support on climate plan.

text.p: President Bill Clinton launched a campaign on Thursday to win U.S. support for a global treaty to trim carbon pollution from the burning of oil, coal and gas and help slow down climate changes.

Facing opposition from powerful industries that produce or rely on cheap energy, the White House is trying to convince the American public to back a plan to limit carbon emissions in industrialised countries in a treaty to be signed in Kyoto, Japan at the end of this year.

"We see the train coming. But most ordinary Americans in their daily lives can't hear the whistle blowing," Clinton said at an unprecedented White House gathering of seven leading scientists, including three Nobel prize winners, to make the public more aware of the impact of global warming.

He said the United States had to commit to "realistic and binding limits" on greenhouse gas emissions at the Kyoto conference, rather than delaying action. "The longer you wait, the more disruptive the ultimate resolution will be."
Oil and coal companies, automakers, utilities and other industries disagree, saying scientists do not yet know enough about global warming to warrant drastic moves to combat it.
They said the American public would not fall for Clinton's "photo-op" Thursday if it was going to cost jobs.

"Mr. Clinton will have to balance the vast scientific uncertainty surrounding this issue with the very real economic pain Americans will suffer if he puts politics ahead of good judgment," said Gail McDonald, president of industry groups' Global Climate Coalition.
But the experts at the White House meeting said action should not be delayed just because there is some uncertainty about the extent of global warming caused by human activities.
Harvard environmental scientist John Holdren compared the impact of soaring world fossil fuel use to a mammoth ship, saying: "We know that the supertanker is heading for a reef."

He said those who argue that there is no need to change course because scientists have not quantified the human role in climate change are essentially advocating: "Since this whole supertanker business is proceeding in the fog, we should feel better about it."

The majority of the world's climate experts predict that the earth's surface temperature will rise by about 3.5 degrees Fahrenheit over the next century. By comparison, the earth's temperature has risen about 9 degrees since the last Ice Age.

The scientists warned that warming of the atmosphere will lead to higher sea levels and flooding, which could wipe out some coastal areas, and lead to more droughts and floods in other areas, affecting croplands.

"No nation will escape from the troubles of pressure on world food supply," said Henry Kendall, a Nobel laureate physicist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, adding that food shortages would trigger vast migrations of people.
The White House plans to hold more meetings with policy groups and host a conference this fall on climate change, to build consensus for the international climate treaty.

Part of the opposition to the treaty centres on the fact that industrialised countries have agreed to curb their own emissions before imposing requirements on developing countries, whose pollution is expected to surpass levels in the rich countries within the next 25 years.

Industry groups say developing countries should be subject to the same carbon emissions cuts as industrialised nations, otherwise companies operating in the rich nations will be at a competitive disadvantage.
